title: The Sudden Attack from a Different Side
subtitle: Tie down the rooks, then change wings

source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter V, §26 The Sudden Attack from a Different Side, Example 56

narration.say: Black has the more mobile rooks. White must protect the isolated pawns on a3 and c3.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Check along the fourth rank.

feedback.*: Move the rook from c4 to e4.

exercise.hint: Move the rook from c4 to e4.

narration.say: Rook to a4. White defends a3 with rook to a2.
Black advances h5, preparing h4 and fixing another target.
White moves the rook to d1. Black doubles pressure on the a-file.
White returns the rook to a1. Black advances h4.
White brings the king toward the queenside pawns. Black improves the king.
White hopes to free the rooks by defending the pawns with the king. Black changes the point of attack.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Transfer the rook on a5 to the kingside.
exercise.success: 7...Rg5! The attack shifts to the kingside.

narration.say: White has played Rg1. Capablanca calls this a serious mistake. Black moves the rook to f4.
White brings the king to d3. Black can penetrate with check.

exercise.prompt: Black to move. Invade the third rank with check.
exercise.success: 9...Rf3+! White moves the king to e2.

steps.title: Do not invent the final moves

narration.say: The book ends this line here and says Black won a few moves later. We stop at the same position.
The principle is greater mobility: tie the opposing rooks to pawns, then move your attack to the other wing.

steps.source: Black, therefore, makes a plan to shift the attack to the King’s side at the proper time, in order to obtain some advantage from the greater mobility of his Rooks.
